Watergate. The scandal that exposed abuse of presidential power and fundamentally altered how America viewed its government.

On June 17, 1972, five burglars were arrested breaking into the Democratic National Committee offices at the Watergate complex in Washington, D.C. It happened during the presidential campaign. At first, it seemed like a minor incident. But it wasn't.

The break-in was directly connected to CREEP, the Committee to Re-elect the President. CREEP orchestrated the burglary and many other illegal campaign activities. This wasn't just a crime. It was a systematic operation.

President Nixon and his advisors then made it worse. They engaged in a cover-up. They destroyed evidence. They tried to obstruct the FBI investigation. These cover-up crimes ended up being worse than the original break-in. They revealed an abuse of presidential power itself.

Two Washington Post reporters named Bob Woodward and Carl Bernstein broke the story open. Their source was Deep Throat, who turned out to be Mark Felt, the FBI's Deputy Director. Felt leaked crucial information that exposed the scandal layer by layer.

The House Judiciary Committee voted to impeach Nixon on three counts: obstruction of justice, abuse of power, and contempt of Congress. The evidence was overwhelming. Nixon faced almost certain conviction in a Senate trial.

So Nixon resigned on August 9, 1974. He was the only U.S. president to ever resign from office. Gerald Ford took over as president and later issued an unconditional pardon.

But the scandal's impact extended far beyond just Nixon's resignation. It triggered major reforms. Congress passed the War Powers Act. Campaign finance laws changed with the Federal Election Campaign Act. A new independent counsel statute was created. The scandal showed America that the system could work, that the checks and balances written into the Constitution were real and could be enforced.

Richard Nixon was the president whose abuse of power precipitated the scandal. Gerald Ford was his successor who pardoned him. The White House itself became synonymous with the cover-up and obstructionism. And the scandal catalyzed renewed focus on constitutional checks on executive power, a lesson that resonates to this day.
